references.text: The hardening of Pharaoh's heart by the Lord is a recurring theme first introduced here, where God tells Moses that He will make Pharaoh's heart unyielding.
God declares that He will harden Pharaoh's heart and perform many signs and wonders in Egypt, the same theme as in 14:4.
Repeats the theme of hardening the Egyptians' hearts and that God will be glorified through Pharaoh and his army, so that the Egyptians may know that He is the Lord.
God explains the purpose of raising up Pharaoh: to display His power and so that His name may be proclaimed throughout the earth.
The same expression that God will show Himself great and holy and make Himself known to many nations, so that they may know that He is the Lord.
God glorifies Himself through His mighty deeds, parallel to how He was glorified through Pharaoh.
Paul cites the story of Pharaoh as an example of God's sovereign will in hardening whom He wills, with a direct reference to Exodus 2.
The expression 'you shall know that I am the Lord' is used regarding Israel's recognition of God, parallel to the Egyptians' recognition in 14:4.
The Egyptians shall know that the Lord is God when He stretches out His hand against Egypt, the same purpose as in 14:4.
Direct continuation of the same prophetic statement about God's glorification through judgment on Egypt.
Theological parallel: God's judgment on Egypt results in the nation knowing Him as the Lord.
Direct conclusion to the same prophecy: Glorification through judgment leads to recognition of the Lord.
Theological contrast: Recognition of the Lord as a result of judgment on enemies versus given to God's people for repentance.
Direct allusion: Uses Pharaoh's hardening as a historical example of God's power and judgment.
Theological parallel: Judgment on Egypt as a means to cause them to know the Lord.
Theological parallel: Judgment on Egypt (via Babylon) leads to recognition of the Lord's sovereignty.
